Ernst & Young discloses data breach after support system hack

Ernst & Young is notifying clients that a third-party support ticket system used by its IT staff was accessed by an unauthorized party, who downloaded documents that may contain client tax-related personal and financial information. EY says it has secured the system, notified law enforcement, and is offering affected clients 24 months of Experian identity monitoring.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Ernst & Young is notifying customers of a data breach caused by the compromise of a third-party support ticket system used by its IT personnel.
  • 02The company determined that an unauthorized third party accessed the support platform between March 28 and April 12 and downloaded multiple documents.
  • 03The exposed information included certain personal and financial data contained in or used to prepare tax filings, but the specific data types remain unclear.
  • 04Ernst & Young has not disclosed how many customers were affected or whether the incident impacts only U.S. customers or customers in other countries.
  • 05Ernst & Young says it secured its systems, notified federal law enforcement, and is offering affected clients 24 months of identity monitoring and restoration services through Experian.

Ernst & Young is notifying customers of a data breach after a third-party support ticket system used by its IT personnel was compromised. The company said support tickets submitted through the platform may have included documents containing client tax information. EY is one of the world’s four largest auditing and professional services providers, with operations in more than 150 countries.

According to the breach notification, EY detected anomalous activity on its networks on April 23 and began an investigation. With help from external cybersecurity experts, the company determined that an unauthorized third party accessed the platform between March 28 and April 12 and downloaded multiple documents. The affected information included certain personal and financial data contained in or used to prepare tax filings, though the specific exposed data types remain unclear.

EY has not disclosed how many customers were affected or whether the incident impacts only U.S. customers or other countries as well. The company said it secured its systems, notified federal law enforcement, and removed the unauthorized access. EY said it is not aware of misuse or further exposure of the stolen files and is offering affected clients 24 months of identity monitoring and restoration services through Experian.

  • The incident shows that support ticket systems can hold highly sensitive client tax documents, even when they are not the primary systems used for tax filing work.
  • EY detected anomalous activity on April 23, after the unauthorized access window of March 28 to April 12 had already ended.
  • The public notice leaves major exposure details unresolved because the sample notification uses placeholders for specific data types and EY has not disclosed the number or location of affected customers.
  • No ransomware or data extortion group had claimed responsibility at the time of publication, despite the theft of multiple documents.

Ernst & Young says someone broke into a third-party support ticket system used by its IT staff and downloaded documents from support requests. Some of those documents may have included clients’ tax-related personal and financial information, though the company has not said how many customers were affected or whether the impact is limited to the United States. This matters because exposed tax and financial details can put people at risk of identity theft or fraud, so EY is offering affected clients 24 months of Experian identity monitoring and restoration services.

Microsoft announced that Windows Server 2022 will reach the end of mainstream support on October 13, 2026. The October 2026 security update will be the last mainstream support update for this version. After that date, Windows Server 2022 will move to extended support and continue receiving monthly security updates at no additional cost through October 14, 2031.

Windows Server 2022 was first announced in March 2021 and became generally available in September 2021 as a Long-Term Servicing Channel release with 10 years of support. Microsoft is advising customers to upgrade to Windows Server 2025, the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel release for Windows Server, to keep environments protected and supported with full mainstream support. Windows Server 2025 became generally available in November 2024 and can be tested through a free 180-day trial from the Microsoft Evaluation Center.

Windows Server 2025 will reach the end of mainstream support on November 13, 2029, with extended support ending on November 14, 2034.   • Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition has a different timeline for hotpatching than the general mainstream support deadline, with hotpatching extended until October 2027.
  • Moving to Windows Server 2025 provides a longer support timeline than staying on Windows Server 2022, with mainstream support ending on November 13, 2029 and extended support ending on November 14, 2034.

Microsoft says Windows Server 2022 will leave its main support period on October 13, 2026, but it will still get free security updates until October 14, 2031. This affects organizations using Windows Server 2022, which is software that runs many business computer systems behind the scenes. Microsoft is urging those customers to start testing and planning a move to Windows Server 2025 so their systems stay protected and fully supported.

HollowByte DDoS flaw bloats OpenSSL server memory with 11-byte payload

A DoS flaw dubbed HollowByte lets unauthenticated attackers bloat OpenSSL server memory with only an 11-byte TLS payload, potentially leaving services permanently memory-heavy until restarted. OpenSSL has fixed it in 4.0.1 and backported patches to 3.6.3, 3.5.7, 3.4.6, and 3.0.21, so organizations should update promptly.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A vulnerability dubbed HollowByte allows unauthenticated attackers to trigger a denial-of-service condition on OpenSSL servers with a malicious payload of just 11 bytes.
  • 02Vulnerable OpenSSL versions allocate memory based on the length declared in a TLS handshake header before receiving and validating the payload.
  • 03Okta researchers said repeated connections with randomized claimed sizes can fragment the heap and cause a server’s Resident Set Size to climb continuously, with a restart required to fully reclaim the space.
  • 04The OpenSSL library is embedded in software such as NGINX, Apache, Node.js, Python, Ruby, PHP, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, and is pre-installed on most Linux distributions for TLS encryption and certificate handling.
  • 05The issue has been fixed in OpenSSL 4.0.1 and backported to versions 3.6.3, 3.5.7, 3.4.6, and 3.0.21.

A vulnerability dubbed HollowByte allows unauthenticated attackers to trigger a denial-of-service condition on OpenSSL servers using a malicious payload of just 11 bytes. The OpenSSL team has fixed the issue without assigning an identifier and has backported the patch to older releases. Because OpenSSL is widely used as a foundation for secure internet communication, the article says organizations should prioritize moving to a fixed version.

Okta’s Red Team explained that vulnerable OpenSSL versions allocate memory based on the size declared in a TLS handshake header before receiving and checking the actual payload. An attacker can open TLS connections and send an 11-byte input whose header claims a much larger message body will follow, causing the server to allocate memory and then wait for data that never arrives. Repeating this across multiple connections can consume significant memory with relatively little transmitted data.

Okta reported that glibc may keep freed small-to-medium memory allocations for reuse instead of immediately returning them to the operating system, which can leave the server bloated even after connections drop. In Okta’s NGINX tests, low-capacity environments could be depleted of memory, while higher-spec servers could lose up to 25% of memory while attack bandwidth stayed below security alerting thresholds. The issue is fixed in OpenSSL 4.0.1 and backported to 3.6.3, 3.5.7, 3.4.6, and 3.0.21, which grow buffers only when data arrives.

  • The attack can stay below security alerting thresholds while still causing higher-spec servers to lose up to 25% of their memory, according to Okta’s NGINX tests.
  • The memory impact can persist even after attacker connections drop because glibc may keep freed small-to-medium allocations for reuse instead of immediately returning them to the operating system.
  • OpenSSL treated the change as a hardening fix rather than a security vulnerability, so defenders may need to look for fixed package versions rather than relying on a vulnerability identifier.
  • The patch changes OpenSSL’s behavior so buffers grow only as data actually arrives, directly removing the trust in the size claimed by the handshake header.

The article describes a problem called HollowByte in OpenSSL, software widely used to keep internet connections secure, where an outsider can send just 11 bytes of data and make a server use up much more memory. This can affect services that rely on OpenSSL, including web servers like NGINX and Apache, programming platforms such as Node.js, Python, Ruby, and PHP, and databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL. In the real world, attackers could slow or disrupt online services without sending much data, and some servers may stay bloated until restarted. OpenSSL has fixed the issue in newer and backported versions, and Okta recommends updating OpenSSL packages immediately.

Inside the Search for "Clean" Residential Proxies for Carding

Criminal carding actors increasingly see residential proxies as only one fragile part of a broader identity-simulation setup, prioritizing “clean” IP reputation, precise location matching, and browser/device consistency. Defenders should not trust residential traffic by default and should focus on cross-session signals like fingerprints, billing data, behavior, and transaction velocity.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Flare researchers analyzed 2,889 unique underground posts from the past two years across about 545 discussion threads about residential proxies and carding.
  • 02Carders increasingly distinguish between “clean” and “dirty” residential proxy pools based on prior use, reputation scores, and whether financial services have blocked the addresses.
  • 03Underground discussions show actors trying to match proxy location with stolen identity details such as billing ZIP code, device time zone, operating-system language, and browser characteristics.
  • 04Residential proxies are frequently discussed alongside antidetect browsers, isolated devices, cookie history, WebRTC configuration, Canvas and WebGL fingerprints, and user-agent consistency.
  • 05The article says defenders should treat residential traffic as context rather than proof that a user is legitimate, and should evaluate consistency across device history, account age, browser fingerprint, payment information, billing information, transaction velocity, and behavior after checkout.

Flare researchers analyzed 2,889 unique underground posts from the past two years across about 545 discussion threads to understand how criminal carding actors use and evaluate residential proxies. The article says these actors no longer treat residential IP addresses as a reliable bypass by themselves, but as one part of a broader setup that includes device fingerprints, browser profiles, billing data, time zones, cookies, and transaction behavior. The article highlights that carders are trying to construct a coherent digital identity rather than simply hide their real IP address. For defenders, the main takeaway is that residential traffic should be treated as context rather than proof of legitimacy, with stronger signals coming from consistency across device history, account age, browser fingerprint, payment details, billing information, velocity, and behavior after checkout.

The article explains that criminals who use stolen payment cards are no longer relying only on home-looking internet connections to appear legitimate online. This matters because banks, payment companies, merchants, and ordinary people can be affected when criminals use these methods for fraud, account takeovers, and abusive traffic. The activity focuses on long-term access and intelligence gathering. GoSerpent contacts an external server and deploys secondary payloads for sensitive data collection and credential dumping.

The malware receives encrypted and Base64-encoded command-line arguments containing the command-and-control address and communication password. It can alert the server of an active infection, open and close listening ports, connect to remote servers, spawn a shell, transfer files, start a SOCKS5 proxy, and forward traffic to connected nodes. Kaspersky said the backdoor can deploy tools including ThumbcacheService, Mimikatz, and QuarksDumpLocalHash.

After months of covert data harvesting, the attackers returned in May 2026 with additional tools including Stowaway, TmcLoader, and TmcPayload to support proxying, remote access, and exfiltration of stored sensitive data. The article also notes a separate Cyderes Howler Cell report on a DoNot Team espionage operation targeting Bangladesh’s military and defence establishments with spear-phishing emails carrying a malicious RTF document.

CVE-2026-58644 is a critical deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.8. The European Commission ordered Google to give rival AI assistants the same reach into Android that Gemini already has, including access to the camera, microphone, screen contents, wake word functionality, and the ability to drive other apps in the background. Google must ship the changes in Android 18 and by 1 August 2027 at the latest. The Android decision is one of two binding specification decisions under the Digital Markets Act, with the second requiring Google to provide anonymised Search query, click, and ranking data to rival search engines and AI chatbots that do search.

The Android decision covers 11 operating system features, five of which Google may place behind certification through a Qualified AI Assistant Programme. Six other features, including ambient data, always-on hotword detection, system-level on-device models, third-party model implementation, and background execution, carry no certification requirement. Ambient data includes microphone input, system audio, camera, screen contents, location, and sensors, continuously and in the background, under the same consent prompts that Google’s own AI services get.

Seven Malicious Vite npm Packages Use Blockchain C2 to Deliver a RAT

Researchers found seven malicious npm packages impersonating Vite tooling that use resilient blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure to deliver a remote access trojan. Developers who installed them should remove the packages, audit systems, rotate credentials, and check shell profile files for persistence.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cybersecurity researchers discovered seven malicious npm packages targeting developers in the Vite frontend tooling ecosystem as part of a software supply chain attack.
  • 02Checkmarx named the campaign ViteVenom and linked it to an expansion of ChainVeil, attributing the activity to a threat actor called SuccessKey.
  • 03The packages were published between June 29 and July 3, 2026, and used scoped names intended to impersonate the @vitejs/* namespace.
  • 04The malicious code runs when imported and retrieves later-stage payloads through blockchain-based infrastructure involving Tron, Aptos, and Binance Smart Chain.
  • 05Users who installed the packages are advised to remove them immediately, audit dependencies, rotate all credentials, and check .bashrc, .zshrc, and .profile for unauthorized modifications.

Cybersecurity researchers discovered seven malicious npm packages targeting the Vite frontend tooling ecosystem as part of a software supply chain attack. Checkmarx named the campaign ViteVenom and described it as an expansion of ChainVeil, which used blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure to deliver a remote access trojan. The activity has been attributed to a threat actor named SuccessKey, with evidence of related malicious activity dating back to February 27, 2026.

The packages were published between June 29 and July 3, 2026, and used scoped names intended to resemble the @vitejs/* namespace. The article lists packages including @uw010010/vite-tree, @vite-tab/tab, @vite-ln/build-ts, @vite-mcp/vite-type, @vite-pro/vite-ui, @vitets/vite-ts, and @vite-ts/vite-ui. Unlike ChainVeil’s unscoped typosquats, ViteVenom focused specifically on developers building applications with the Vite JavaScript and frontend build tool.

The malicious code executes at import time rather than install time and acts as a loader that queries blockchain infrastructure to obtain the next stage. It uses Tron, Aptos, and Binance Smart Chain infrastructure to retrieve and decrypt payload data, with fallback mechanisms including Aptos and direct HTTP retrieval from the command-and-control server. Users who installed the packages are advised to remove them immediately, audit dependencies, rotate all credentials, and check .bashrc, .zshrc, and .profile files for unauthorized modifications.

  • ViteVenom does not execute its malicious code at install time but at import time, which the article says limits endpoint security detections.
  • The campaign uses scoped package names to resemble the @vitejs/* namespace, a shift from ChainVeil’s earlier unscoped typosquats and a tactic meant to appear more legitimate to Vite developers.
  • The blockchain setup is resilient because payload pointers are stored in public blockchain transaction data rather than domain names that can be seized.
  • The malware has multiple retrieval paths: Tron is the primary method, Aptos is a backup, and a separate HTTP fallback can fetch the RAT directly from the C2 server.
  • Checkmarx says differences in package names, maintainer accounts, Tier-1 wallets, and malicious file paths are consistent with one operator compartmentalizing multiple distribution tracks to reduce exposure.

Researchers found seven harmful npm packages aimed at developers who use the Vite tool to build web apps. If a developer added one of these packages to a project, it could secretly fetch more harmful code, steal credentials and files, open remote access to the computer, and make changes that help it stay there. The attackers hid instructions for the harmful code inside public blockchain transactions, which makes the setup very hard to shut down. Anyone who installed the packages is advised to remove them, review their dependencies, change credentials, and check certain shell profile files for unauthorized changes.

ACR Stealer Uses ClickFix Lures to Steal Browser Tokens and Microsoft 365 Files

ACR Stealer campaigns are using ClickFix lures that trick users into pasting commands into Windows Run, leading to theft of browser passwords, session tokens, Microsoft 365 files, and synced OneDrive/SharePoint data. Because stolen tokens remain valid after password resets, defenders should revoke tokens and block the paste-and-run execution path.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft reported that ACR Stealer activity increased across customer environments from late April to mid-June and that campaigns are using ClickFix lures to steal browser credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents.
  • 02The fileless delivery chain starts when a pasted command launches mshta.exe to retrieve remote HTA content, then uses scripts and a JPEG-hosted payload to execute malware in memory.
  • 03ACR Stealer targets Chrome and Edge data stores, uses DPAPI to decrypt saved passwords, cookies, and tokens, and also steals PDFs from the Desktop and Downloads folders.
  • 04A second delivery chain pulls a DLL from a WebDAV share, uses obfuscated PowerShell and a bundled pythonw.exe, persists through a hidden scheduled task, and clears PowerShell history.
  • 05Microsoft’s remediation guidance says suspected victims should isolate affected hosts, rotate credentials, revoke tokens, and check outbound connections to remote shares and image-hosting services.

ACR Stealer, an infostealer active since 2024, is being delivered through ClickFix lures that convince users to paste a command into the Windows Run box and press Enter. Microsoft said its Defender Experts team observed ACR Stealer activity increase across customer environments from late April to mid-June. The campaigns are stealing saved browser passwords, live session tokens, PDFs, Microsoft 365 documents, and files from synced OneDrive and SharePoint folders.

Microsoft described two delivery chains: one that runs almost entirely in memory and another that leaves more traces on disk. The fileless chain uses mshta.exe, remote HTA content, VBScript, PowerShell, and a JPEG-hosted payload that is extracted, decrypted, decompressed, and reflectively executed. The disk-based chain pulls a DLL from a WebDAV share, uses obfuscated PowerShell and pythonw.exe, persists through a hidden scheduled task, copies timestamps from notepad.exe, and clears PowerShell history.

  • 04Okta's NGINX testing reportedly caused a 1 GB server to be OOM-killed with 547 MB frozen in fragments and locked up 25% of memory on a 16 GB server without exceeding connection limits.
  • 05The fix covers TLS only, while the article states that the DTLS handshake path still sizes its buffer from the peer-declared length in OpenSSL 4.0.1.

Okta’s Red Team disclosed HollowByte, an OpenSSL denial-of-service flaw that can make an unpatched server reserve up to 131 KB of memory after receiving an 11-byte TLS request. The issue affects releases on the OpenSSL 4.0, 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, and 3.0 branches before the June 9 fixed versions 4.0.1, 3.6.3, 3.5.7, 3.4.6, and 3.0.21. OpenSSL shipped the fix without a CVE, advisory, or changelog entry identifying it.

The flaw occurs because older OpenSSL versions grew the TLS receive buffer based on the length declared in a handshake header before the message body arrived or handshake checks ran. For an inbound ClientHello, the allocation ceiling is 131 KB, and the worker thread then waits for a body that never comes. Okta said that on glibc systems it tested, freed buffers were not returned to the kernel, so varied connection sizes caused heap fragmentation and persistent resident memory growth.

Okta reported that in NGINX testing, a 1 GB server was OOM-killed with 547 MB of memory frozen in fragments, and a 16 GB server had 25% of system memory locked up without exceeding the connection ceiling. The article says this makes standard connection-limiting defenses insufficient and complicates downstream patch tracking because packages may be backported without changing their OpenSSL version string. The fix covers TLS only, while the article states that DTLS was left unchanged and still sizes its buffer from the peer-declared length in OpenSSL 4.0.1.

  • Standard vulnerability scanners and patch pipelines may miss HollowByte because OpenSSL did not assign it a CVE, publish an advisory, or call it out in the changelog.
  • Checking only the reported OpenSSL version may be unreliable for downstream Linux packages because vendors such as Red Hat often backport fixes while keeping the older version string.
  • Connection limits alone may not prevent the issue, because Okta reported that memory remained fragmented after connections closed and did not require exceeding the connection ceiling.
  • Organizations that build OpenSSL themselves have a clearer remediation path than many downstream users: upgrade to the June 9 fixed releases and restart processes that loaded the old library.
  • The article highlights a classification inconsistency because OpenSSL assigned CVEs to other memory-exhaustion issues in the same release cycle while treating HollowByte as only a bug or hardening fix.

Okta reported a problem in OpenSSL, widely used software that helps servers make secure connections, where a tiny 11-byte request can make an unpatched server set aside memory for data that never arrives. Servers running affected OpenSSL versions before the June 9 fixes can slowly lose usable memory and may eventually be shut down by the operating system. This matters because OpenSSL fixed it without a public vulnerability number or advisory, so many organizations may not realize they need to check whether their servers actually received the patch.

A fake email pretended to be a Chase secure message, claimed to use Virtru, but was actually sent from a LinkedIn address and used links wrapped by Mimecast, making several familiar names appear together to seem trustworthy. It reached an organization’s mailboxes and targeted finance-related users with a generic payment message, trying to get people to click and give up credentials. Elastic Security Labs discovered a new DPRK-aligned Contagious Interview campaign, tracked as REF9403, after a fake recruiter targeted its community Slack workspace with a job posting and coding challenge. The trojanized projects were fully functional e-commerce templates, but they silently executed malicious code when users ran the server. Elastic said the activity overlaps with prior reporting on OTTERCOOKIE based on code similarity, behavior, and related infrastructure.

The campaign matters because developers are the direct targets, and a compromised developer machine can provide attackers with access to credentials, keys, wallets, files, and potentially downstream organizations. The payload delivered four main capabilities: a browser credential and crypto wallet stealer, a file stealer, a Socket.IO-based remote access trojan, and a clipboard stealer. The malware collected browser login data, wallet extension databases, sensitive files, shell histories, cloud and SSH configuration paths, and macOS keychain data.

A key technique in the infection chain was hiding Base64 payload fragments inside HTML comments across SVG flag images in the project’s assets directory. A JavaScript file reassembled the fragments in alphabetical order, decoded them with a custom Base64 function, and executed the result with eval during server startup. Elastic also observed command-and-control activity using rightwidth[.]dev subdomains, including upload endpoints, a Socket.IO controller, and Windows second-stage download paths.

  • The trojanized repositories had zero antivirus detections at the time of writing, showing that benign-looking coding assignments can evade standard file reputation checks even when they contain active credential theft and remote access code.
  • The campaign used fully functional e-commerce projects copied from legitimate templates, so a project running correctly was not evidence that it was safe.
  • The malware avoided simple detection patterns by hiding payload fragments in SVG comments and decoding them with a custom Base64 function before using eval, rather than relying on common decoding methods such as Buffer.from or atob.
  • The file stealer’s exclusion list deliberately avoided many common developer and AI-coding-tool directories such as .claude, .cursor, .gemini, and .windsurf, indicating the attackers tuned collection to reduce noise on developer systems.
  • The malware tagged virtual machines and sandboxes in its command-and-control response but did not stop running, which means analysis environments may still observe behavior while operators can separately prioritize likely real victims.

Elastic Security Labs found a North Korea-linked campaign where fake recruiters offered developers coding challenges that contained hidden harmful code inside image files. Developers who ran these projects could have their saved browser passwords, crypto wallet data, personal files, and clipboard contents stolen, while the attackers also gained remote access to the computer. This matters because one compromised developer can give attackers a starting point to reach the organizations and software projects that depend on that developer’s work.
